document.title: How to Play Blades in the Dark
document.file_purpose: A structured, original learning and table-reference guide for the current official core rules, with a clearly separated note about the optional Deep Cuts expansion.
audience: returning groups needing a rules refresher
software or knowledge-base projects that need structured rules guidance

included: action, fortune, resistance, engagement, vice, downtime, incarceration, and advancement procedures
position, effect, consequences, harm, stress, trauma, armor, clocks, teamwork, factions, coin, and stash
publicly confirmed status and scope of Blades in the Dark: Deep Cuts v1.2
excluded_or_condensed: ritual and crafting subsystems beyond a brief orientation
the paid Deep Cuts rules text

edition_resolution.base_game: Blades in the Dark remains the current core game and is not presented by the publisher as a numbered second edition.
edition_resolution.official_learning_material: The official downloads page links the core play sheets and a player kit whose PDF filename identifies it as v8.2.
edition_resolution.latest_official_rules_expansion: Blades in the Dark: Deep Cuts v1.2, announced as the final version on 2025-11-20.
edition_resolution.how_this_file_uses_latest: This guide teaches the stable core rules as the default playable system. Deep Cuts is treated as a modular, optional expansion rather than silently replacing the core rules.

copyright_and_license_note.status: Unofficial educational rules summary. It is not a replacement for the official book or paid expansion.
copyright_and_license_note.srd_attribution: This work is based on Blades in the Dark, product of One Seven Design, developed and authored by John Harper, and uses material summarized from the Blades in the Dark System Reference Document under Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Unported.
copyright_and_license_note.trademark_note: Blades in the Dark is a trademark of One Seven Design. No endorsement is implied.

system_overview.one_sentence_pitch: Play daring scoundrels who conduct scores, endure consequences, and build a criminal crew amid rival factions, law enforcement, industry, and the supernatural.

default_setting.name: Doskvol
default_setting.summary: A haunted industrial-fantasy city where criminal crews operate under constant pressure from stronger factions and the authorities.
default_setting.setting_dependence: The core procedures can support other Forged in the Dark settings, but the official playbooks, factions, equipment, and examples assume Doskvol.

what_play_is_about: Choosing ambitious goals rather than following a prewritten plot.
Starting operations in motion instead of planning every contingency.
Making risky choices, accepting consequences, and using stress to resist or push harder.
Developing both individual scoundrels and the shared crew.
Letting faction reactions and downtime fallout create the next opportunities.

recommended_group.players: Commonly 2-5 player characters plus one GM; the procedures also work with smaller or larger groups if spotlight and stress economy are watched.
recommended_group.session_length: The official overview describes sessions as roughly 2-6 hours.
recommended_group.campaign_style: Episodic scores linked by persistent character, crew, faction, heat, and project changes.

materials: Pencils or a digital sheet capable of marking clocks and boxes.
The official core book or SRD for edge cases and full setting material.

players: Describe what their scoundrels do and what outcome they want.
Choose the action rating that matches the fictional method they describe.
Choose whether to push, accept a Devil's Bargain, assist, protect, set up, lead a group action, flash back, or resist.
Track stress, trauma, harm, armor, load, coin, stash, and experience.
Have final say over whether their own play matched experience triggers.
game_master: Portray the world, factions, NPCs, threats, and consequences honestly.
Decide when uncertainty and danger require a roll.
Set position and effect for action rolls after hearing the player's method and goal.
Choose and describe consequences that follow from the established threat.
Use fortune rolls and clocks rather than predetermining outcomes.
Present opportunities and follow the consequences instead of scripting a story.
shared_judgment: Everyone contributes to the conversation and can question assumptions.
Players choose their approach and action; the GM evaluates danger and impact.
The table should make the fictional situation clear before dice are rolled.
Rules judgments should preserve established fiction rather than override it without explanation.

session_zero.purpose: Agree on the kind of criminal drama the group wants before creating a crew whose activities may include violence, coercion, vice, imprisonment, and supernatural horror.
recommended_agenda: Choose the desired tone: adventurous caper, grim crime drama, occult horror, political intrigue, or a blend.
Identify subjects that should be absent, kept off-screen, or handled lightly.
Agree on a pause or rewind method for uncomfortable material.
Clarify how graphic violence, coercion, drugs, addiction, imprisonment, and harm to bystanders will be portrayed.
Decide how much player-versus-player conflict is welcome; require player consent before character conflict removes another player's meaningful control.
Choose the crew type and identify activities the group is excited to see repeatedly.
Create a shared understanding that setbacks generate new play rather than ending the campaign.
session_zero.note: These are modern facilitation recommendations rather than a replacement for the official rules.

phases.name: free_play
phases.purpose: Characters talk, pursue interests, gather information, meet contacts, and choose or create opportunities.
phases.exit_condition: The group identifies a target and goal for an operation.

phases.name: score
phases.purpose: Choose a plan and detail, make the engagement roll, cut directly to the first obstacle, use action rolls, teamwork, flashbacks, resistance, and clocks until the operation is resolved.
phases.exit_condition: The operation succeeds, fails, is abandoned, or transforms into a different situation.

phases.name: downtime
phases.purpose: Resolve payoff, heat, entanglements, personal recovery and projects, vice, and faction movement.
phases.exit_condition: Downtime choices are complete and new opportunities emerge.

phases.name: return_to_free_play
phases.purpose: Play scenes arising from downtime and choose the next score.

game_structure.important_rule: The phases organize procedures; they are not hard barriers. Ordinary roleplay and action rolls can occur during downtime, while downtime mechanics may sometimes be invoked when fiction provides the opportunity.
typical_session_flow: Review the current situation and unresolved clocks.
Play free scenes or gather information.
Choose a target, goal, plan type, and required plan detail.
Determine payoff, rep, heat, wanted changes, and entanglement.
Take downtime activities and advance faction clocks.
Review character and crew experience triggers.

core_dice_system.pool_method: Roll a number of d6 equal to the relevant rating plus applicable bonus dice, then read the single highest die.
core_dice_system.zero_dice_rule: At zero or fewer dice, roll 2d6 and keep the lower die. A zero-die roll cannot produce a critical.

result_bands.critical: Two or more sixes. The result is better than an ordinary full success, usually through increased effect or another added advantage.

probability_interpretation: A single die is intentionally risky: half of rolls land in the 1-3 band.
Two or three dice make outright bad results less common, but mixed results remain frequent.
The game expects consequences and resistance to appear regularly; avoiding all consequences is not the normal play pattern.

primary_roll_types.name: action_roll
primary_roll_types.used_when: A player character acts toward a goal while a dangerous or troublesome threat opposes them.

primary_roll_types.name: fortune_roll
primary_roll_types.used_when: The GM needs an uncertain answer and no player-facing action or resistance roll applies.

primary_roll_types.name: resistance_roll
primary_roll_types.used_when: A player rejects or reduces a consequence already announced by the GM.

primary_roll_types.name: downtime_roll
primary_roll_types.used_when: A core downtime activity measures quality, progress, recovery, or stress relief.
primary_roll_types.uses_effect: Uses result levels or activity-specific outputs rather than action-roll position.

primary_roll_types.name: engagement_roll
primary_roll_types.used_when: The crew begins a score and the table needs to establish the initial position.

actions_and_attributes.attribute_rule: An attribute rating equals the number of actions under that attribute with at least one dot, not the total dots in the attribute.

rating_ranges.action: 0-4; starting characters normally cannot begin above 2, later normally cap at 3 until the crew unlocks Mastery.

Insight.resists: Consequences involving deception, perception, understanding, or mental processing.

Prowess.resists: Consequences involving physical strain, movement, injury, or bodily control.

Resolve.resists: Consequences involving willpower, social pressure, fear, possession, or mental force.

actions.name: Attune
actions.core_intent: Open the mind to supernatural power and the ghost field.
actions.overlap_note: Survey may be safer or clearer for ordinary perception; Attune is appropriate when the method is explicitly arcane.

actions.name: Command
actions.core_intent: Compel immediate obedience through authority, intimidation, or force of presence.
common_uses: issue an order that demands compliance
actions.overlap_note: Consort relies on relationship and standing; Sway relies on manipulation or argument.

actions.name: Consort
actions.core_intent: Socialize through existing relationships, communities, heritage, background, or underworld connections.
actions.overlap_note: Sway is more suitable when the method is deception, guile, or a direct persuasive argument.

actions.name: Finesse
actions.core_intent: Use dexterity, subtle manipulation, precision handling, or graceful control.
common_uses: fight a formal or precise duel
actions.overlap_note: Tinker is usually better for technically manipulating a lock or mechanism; Skirmish is usually better in a chaotic melee.

actions.name: Hunt
actions.core_intent: Track, locate, stalk, or attack a target with planned precision at range.
actions.overlap_note: Survey reads the broader situation; Prowl handles traversal and concealment; Skirmish handles close combat.

actions.name: Prowl
actions.core_intent: Move skillfully, quietly, and athletically through obstacles or concealment.
actions.overlap_note: Skirmish is usually better once a close fight becomes open and contested.

actions.name: Skirmish
actions.core_intent: Engage and control an opponent in close combat.
actions.overlap_note: Finesse may better fit formal precision; Wreck may fit raw destructive force; Prowl may fit a hidden ambush.

actions.name: Study
actions.core_intent: Closely examine details and interpret evidence.
actions.overlap_note: Survey is better for quickly reading a live location or developing situation.

actions.name: Survey
actions.core_intent: Observe a location or situation and anticipate what is happening or about to happen.
actions.overlap_note: Study is more detailed and analytical; Hunt is more focused on a target and its movements.

actions.name: Sway
actions.core_intent: Influence through charm, lies, guile, disguise, logic, or argument.
actions.overlap_note: Consort depends on relationship or social belonging; Command depends on authority or intimidation.

actions.name: Tinker
actions.core_intent: Build, alter, repair, disable, or operate mechanisms through technical work.
actions.overlap_note: Finesse may handle quick manual control; Wreck may be faster when preservation and subtlety do not matter.

actions.name: Wreck
actions.core_intent: Apply destructive force, sabotage, or chaos.
actions.overlap_note: Skirmish is usually better for trading attacks with an active opponent.

actions_and_attributes.player_choice_rule: The player chooses the action by describing the method. The GM does not substitute a different action, but may set worse position or lower effect when the chosen method is poorly suited.

action_roll.trigger: Use an action roll only when a PC's concrete goal conflicts with a dangerous or troublesome threat. Do not roll for harmless routine tasks.

procedure.name: state_goal
procedure.instruction: The player states the concrete outcome they want, not merely the physical motion.

procedure.name: choose_action
procedure.instruction: The player describes the method and chooses the matching action rating.

procedure.name: set_position
procedure.instruction: The GM rates the danger as controlled, risky, or desperate. Risky is the default.

procedure.name: set_effect
procedure.instruction: The GM rates the likely impact as zero, limited, standard, great, or occasionally extreme.

procedure.name: add_bonus_dice
procedure.instruction: Apply assistance and either a push or a Devil's Bargain, plus any special-ability modifiers.

procedure.name: roll_and_resolve
procedure.instruction: Roll the pool, apply the position-specific outcome, narrate the PC's effect, announce consequences, and allow resistance.

assist.limits: Only one assistant may directly add a die to a roll; the assistant must describe meaningful help and may share exposure to consequences.

devils_bargain.cost: A stated complication becomes true regardless of the roll.
devils_bargain.rule: A push for +1d and a Devil's Bargain do not stack with each other on the same action roll.
valid_examples: a troublesome clock starts or advances
devils_bargain.consent: The player may reject or renegotiate a bargain; the GM has final say on validity.

push_for_effect.stacking_note: A character may choose each normal push benefit at most once for a given action; special abilities may add further options.

push_while_incapacitated.benefit: Take an action despite level-3 harm or another incapacitating condition.

controlled.fiction: The PC acts from a dominant or well-prepared advantage.
controlled.critical: Success with increased effect or an extra advantage.
controlled.4_5: The player may withdraw and try another approach, or succeed with a minor consequence such as lesser harm, a small complication, reduced effect, or movement to risky position.
controlled.1_3: The attempt falters; the player may withdraw or seize a riskier opportunity.

risky.fiction: The PC acts under meaningful danger; this is the usual default.
risky.critical: Success with increased effect or an extra advantage.
risky.4_5: Success with one or more consequences appropriate to a risky threat.
risky.1_3: The threat dominates: the PC commonly fails or has weak effect and suffers consequences such as harm, complication, desperate position, or lost opportunity.

desperate.fiction: The PC is overmatched, exposed, or in serious trouble.
desperate.critical: Success with increased effect or an extra advantage.
desperate.4_5: Success with severe harm, a serious complication, reduced effect, or another severe consequence.
desperate.1_3: The worst outcome fitting the established threat, often severe harm, serious complication, and/or loss of the opportunity.
desperate.xp: Mark 1 xp in the attribute containing the rolled action whenever a desperate action roll is made.

action_roll.double_duty_rule: NPCs do not normally make opposing action rolls. One PC action roll resolves both the PC's attempted effect and the threat's response.
narration_order: Before rolling, state goal, method, position, effect, and visible threat.
After rolling, describe the PC's achieved effect.
Apply consequences that do not erase a successful result.
Ask whether the player resists any consequence.
Update clocks and the fictional position.

position_and_effect.position_definition: How dangerous the attempt is and how severe the likely consequences can be.
position_and_effect.effect_definition: How much the successful action changes the situation.

zero.meaning: The action cannot meaningfully affect this obstacle as currently described.
next_steps: obtain more potent or higher-quality means

standard.meaning: The ordinary expected impact of the action.

great.meaning: More than expected, including an added benefit or major progress.

extreme.meaning: An exceptional impact beyond great effect; the GM states what this means in the fiction.
extreme.clock_ticks: Usually more than 3 or completion of an appropriate obstacle, at GM judgment.

effect_factors.potency: A special advantage, vulnerability, arcane force, extra time, or unusually fitting method.
effect_factors.quality: The effectiveness of tools, weapons, gear, or resources; crew Tier often summarizes quality, and a Fine item generally acts as +1 quality.
effect_factors.scale: Numbers, size, area, reach, or scope. Larger scale helps in some situations and hinders in others.

assessment_method: Start with a fast intuitive judgment.
Only compare potency, quality, and scale when the answer is unclear or an advantage matters.
Raise or lower effect for meaningful factor advantages or disadvantages.
Explain the decisive factor in plain fictional terms.
position_and_effect.trade_position_for_effect: After the GM states position and effect, the player may propose taking a worse position for greater effect, or sometimes a safer position for reduced effect, when the fiction supports the trade.
position_and_effect.common_error: Do not treat position as difficulty and effect as success chance. Dice determine the outcome band; position controls danger, while effect controls impact.

consequence_types.name: reduced_effect
consequence_types.meaning: Lower the achieved effect by one level after other factors.

consequence_types.name: complication
consequence_types.meaning: Introduce or escalate trouble, including evidence, heat, reinforcements, lost gear, faction reaction, or a clock.

consequence_types.name: lost_opportunity
consequence_types.meaning: The current route to the goal closes; trying again requires a new method or changed circumstances.

consequence_types.name: worse_position
consequence_types.meaning: The PC loses control and the next attempt begins from a more dangerous position.

consequence_types.name: harm
consequence_types.meaning: A persistent physical, mental, emotional, or supernatural debility.

consequences_resistance_harm_and_armor.success_integrity_rule: A consequence must not erase the effect of a successful 4/5. The PC gets the stated effect, and the consequence changes or worsens the situation around that success.

resistance.timing: After the GM announces a consequence and before play moves past it.
resistance.choice: The player chooses whether to resist; once the roll is made, its stress cost is accepted.
resistance.attribute_selection: The GM chooses Insight, Prowess, or Resolve according to the nature of the consequence.
resistance.dice_pool: Roll dice equal to the selected attribute rating.
resistance.effectiveness: Resistance always works. The GM states whether it reduces severity or avoids the consequence completely.
resistance.stress_cost: 6 minus the highest die. On a critical resistance roll, clear 1 stress.
limits: A specific consequence may be resisted only once.
If several consequences are announced, each may require its own resistance choice and roll.
The player cannot roll first and then decide whether to resist.
resistance.tone_dial: Frequent full avoidance produces a more daring tone; mostly reducing consequences produces a grittier tone.

1.penalty: Reduced effect when the harm applies.

3.penalty: The character needs help or must push themself to act when the harm applies.

4.penalty: Death or a catastrophic permanent outcome unless reduced or otherwise prevented.

harm.overflow: If the row for incoming harm is full, mark it one level higher. Overflow beyond level 3 becomes level 4.
harm.specificity: Name harm concretely so the table can judge when its penalty applies.
harm.new_harm_and_healing: Suffering new harm clears existing ticks on the healing clock under the core rules.

armor.standard_armor: Mark the armor box to reduce or avoid an applicable consequence without a resistance roll.
armor.heavy_armor: Provides an additional armor use when carried; it may reduce a consequence a second step if applicable.
armor.special_armor: Only usable through a playbook or crew ability that explicitly invokes it.
armor.refresh: Armor uses refresh when load is chosen for the next score.

death_and_continuation: An unresisted fatal harm can kill a PC.
A player may create a new scoundrel or promote an existing crew NPC.
Some supernatural continuation options exist in the official game, but their full rules are beyond this introductory guide.

spent_for: self-healing or untreated recovery under the core rules
stress.design_intent: Stress is a player-controlled resource that allows scoundrels to remain capable even when rolls generate serious consequences.

trauma.trigger: When the final stress box is marked, the PC takes one trauma and leaves the current conflict.
trauma.return: The PC later returns with stress cleared and their vice considered satisfied for the next downtime.
trauma.permanence: Trauma conditions are permanent under the core rules.
trauma.retirement: At four trauma conditions, the character is no longer an active daring scoundrel and must retire or take the fall for the crew.

conditions.Cold: Detached from emotional appeals or social bonds.
conditions.Haunted: Distracted or overwhelmed by past horrors and visions.
conditions.Obsessed: Consumed by a person, activity, ideology, or goal.
conditions.Soft: Sentimental, passive, or unwilling to maintain a hard edge.
conditions.Unstable: Volatile, impulsive, frozen, enraged, or despairing.

vice.purpose: Clear stress during downtime through a defined obsession and purveyor.
vice.roll: Roll the PC's lowest attribute rating and clear stress equal to the highest die.
vice.overindulgence_trigger: If the result would clear more stress than is currently marked.
overindulgence_options: Attract Trouble: resolve an additional entanglement.
Lost: play another character until this PC returns; the returning PC has healed their harm.
Tapped: the current vice purveyor cuts the PC off.
vice.ignoring_vice: If a traumatized PC does not or cannot indulge during downtime, take stress equal to the number of trauma conditions.

progress_clocks.definition: A segmented circle that makes progress toward an obstacle, goal, or danger visible.

standard_sizes.6_segments: Complicated or requiring several meaningful steps.
standard_sizes.multiple_clocks: Use layered clocks for especially complex goals rather than one oversized clock.

progress_clocks.naming_rule: Name the obstacle or developing state, not the action method. Example: 'Interior Patrols,' not 'Sneak Past Guards.'

types.danger_clock: Fills as a threat approaches or complications accumulate.
types.racing_clocks: Two sides progress toward opposed endpoints.
types.linked_clocks: Completing one unlocks the next layer.
types.mission_clock: Tracks a shrinking window of opportunity.
types.tug_of_war: Can fill and empty as control changes.
types.long_term_project: Tracks persistent work completed during downtime.
types.faction_clock: Tracks an NPC faction's agenda between scores.

principles: A clock displays the fiction; it does not replace the fiction.
Do not create a clock for a problem that one decisive action can resolve.
Tell players what a clock represents and what happens when it fills unless secrecy itself is important to the fiction.
Advance clocks only when a roll, consequence, downtime result, or fictional event justifies progress.

when_to_use: The outcome concerns people or events outside direct PC action.
No action roll, resistance roll, engagement roll, or downtime procedure applies.
The GM wants uncertainty rather than a predetermined answer.
pool_sources: a relevant PC action rating for information quality
fortune_roll.modifiers: Add or subtract 1d for major advantages or disadvantages.
fortune_roll.opposed_sides: Roll for each side and compare their performance when two NPC forces directly oppose each other.

gather_information.start: The player asks a specific question and explains how the character learns the answer.
gather_information.obstacle_present: Use an action roll because the inquiry itself faces danger or trouble.
gather_information.honesty_rule: The GM answers honestly; effect determines completeness, not truthfulness.

detail_by_effect.limited: Incomplete or partial; more work is required.
detail_by_effect.great: Complete, exceptional, and possibly broader information.

gather_information.complex_investigation: Create a long-term project clock when the question cannot reasonably be answered by one attempt.

core_playbooks.Cutter: Focuses on violence, intimidation, endurance, and command of force.
core_playbooks.Hound: Focuses on tracking, ranged precision, hunting, and an optional trained pet.
core_playbooks.Leech: Focuses on alchemy, gadgets, sabotage, medicine, and technical work.
core_playbooks.Lurk: Focuses on stealth, infiltration, burglary, and daring movement.
core_playbooks.Slide: Focuses on deception, disguise, manipulation, and social leverage.
core_playbooks.Spider: Focuses on planning, contacts, coordination, and conspiracy.
core_playbooks.Whisper: Focuses on spirits, rituals, the ghost field, and supernatural power.

character_creation.playbook_rule: A playbook is a starting focus, ability list, item list, and XP trigger, not an exclusive class. Any scoundrel may attempt any action.

steps.name: choose_playbook
steps.details: Choose the focus and special-ability list that best matches the kind of trouble you want.

steps.name: choose_heritage
steps.details: Describe where the character's family line comes from and add one personal family detail.

steps.name: choose_background
steps.details: Choose what the character did before becoming a scoundrel and add a specific detail.

steps.name: assign_action_dots
steps.details: Begin with the playbook's three printed dots, then add four: one tied to heritage, one tied to background, and two anywhere. No action begins above 2 unless an ability says otherwise.

steps.name: choose_special_ability
steps.details: Choose one ability from the playbook.

steps.name: choose_friend_and_rival
steps.details: Select one listed NPC as a close relationship and another as a rival or enemy.

steps.name: choose_vice
steps.details: Choose a vice category, define the specific obsession, and name its purveyor and location.

steps.name: name_alias_and_look
steps.details: Record identity and a few evocative visual details.

steps.name: review_xp_and_items
steps.details: Read the playbook XP trigger, special items, stress, trauma, harm, armor, and load areas.

loadout.rule: Do not choose every item before the score. Choose a load limit, then mark items when they appear in the fiction until the limit is reached.

levels.light_1_to_3: Fast and inconspicuous; blends with ordinary citizens.
levels.normal_4_to_5: Clearly a scoundrel prepared for trouble.
levels.heavy_6: Slower and visibly equipped for an operation.

loadout.item_boxes: An item with two connected boxes consumes 2 load; italicized or zero-load items consume no load.
loadout.fictional_limit: A declared item must be plausible for the chosen load and current circumstances.

quick_build_advice: Choose the playbook whose XP trigger sounds fun, not merely the one with the highest starting action.
Spread starting dots across attributes if you want stronger resistance pools.
Tie friend, rival, vice, heritage, and background to factions so the GM immediately has material.
Leave some details undefined so play can reveal them.

core_crew_types.Assassins: Kill or capture targets for payment or strategic purpose.
core_crew_types.Bravos: Use violence, extortion, battle, and territorial control.
core_crew_types.Cult: Serve a deity or supernatural power and advance its agenda.
core_crew_types.Hawkers: Sell illicit goods, services, or vice and develop clientele.
core_crew_types.Shadows: Steal, spy, infiltrate, sabotage, and conduct covert operations.
core_crew_types.Smugglers: Transport people or cargo through danger and restricted territory.

steps: Choose a crew type.
Choose an initial reputation and describe the lair.
Establish a small hunting ground and its preferred operation type.
Resolve the relationship with the faction that claims the hunting ground.
Choose one crew special ability.
Take the two printed starting upgrades and choose two additional upgrades.
Apply faction status changes caused by how the upgrades were obtained.
Choose a favorite contact and apply related faction status changes.
Name the crew, define its look or symbol, and summarize immediate rivals and opportunities.

hunting_ground_choices.pay_1_coin: The controlling faction gives the crew room to work.
hunting_ground_choices.pay_2_coin: Gain +1 status with the controlling faction.
hunting_ground_choices.pay_nothing: Take -1 status with the controlling faction.

crew_creation_and_factions.hunting_ground_benefit: For the chosen operation type in the hunting ground, gain +1d to gather information and one free extra downtime activity that contributes to that operation.

tier.meaning: Overall wealth, influence, equipment quality, and organizational scale.

gang_scale.6: about 160 people or another colossal organization

hold.strong: The crew securely occupies its current Tier.
hold.weak: The crew is vulnerable to dropping a Tier if hold is lost again.
hold.war_effect: War temporarily reduces hold by one step.

rep_and_development.tier_adjustment: +1 rep per target Tier above the crew, or -1 per Tier below, minimum 0.
rep_and_development.quiet_operation: If nobody knows the operation happened, earn 0 rep.
rep_and_development.turf: Each turf reduces the rep required for development by 1, to a maximum of 6 turf.
rep_and_development.when_full_with_weak_hold: Reset rep and improve hold to strong.
rep_and_development.when_full_with_strong_hold: Pay new Tier x 8 coin, increase Tier by one, reset rep, and set hold to weak.

faction_status.+3: Allied; will help even at meaningful cost and expects the same.
faction_status.+2: Friendly; helps when it does not create serious problems.
faction_status.+1: Helpful; helps when cost and risk are small.
faction_status.-1: Interfering; exploits low-cost chances to trouble the crew.
faction_status.-2: Hostile; actively seeks chances to hurt the crew.
faction_status.-3: War; prioritizes harming the crew even when costly.

war_rules: Each PC receives only one free downtime activity.
End war through elimination, surrender, or negotiated status change.

claims.acquisition: Choose a claim, learn who controls it, and complete a score to seize it.
claims.status_effect: Seizing a claim usually causes -2 status with the former owner and may improve status with its enemies.
claims.benefit: A seized claim grants its listed benefit while held.
claims.loss: Enemies can seize claims; losing the lair suppresses all claim benefits until a lair is restored.

types.gang: A group whose quality and scale normally equal crew Tier.
types.expert: One skilled NPC with quality normally equal crew Tier plus one.

cohorts.independent_action: Roll cohort quality as a fortune roll.
cohorts.directed_action: A PC may Command the cohort or lead it in a group action.
cohorts.recovery: If recovery is possible, remove one cohort harm during downtime; a PC can spend an activity to help remove an additional level under the core rules.

choose_opportunity: Accept or solicit a job from a patron.
Target a faction asset, weakness, or project.
Pursue a PC or crew long-term goal.
React to an entanglement, rival, or faction move.
running_a_score.planning_rule: Players do not need to enumerate every precaution. The characters are assumed to prepare competently; the engagement roll and flashbacks handle uncertainty and omitted details.

Transport.intent: Move cargo or people through danger.

before_engagement: State the target and concrete objective.
Provide its required detail; gather information if the detail is unknown.
Each PC chooses light, normal, or heavy load.
Identify major engagement advantages and disadvantages.

possible_advantages: friend or contact supplies useful aid
target is lower Tier or otherwise disadvantaged
district, timing, or circumstances strongly favor the crew
possible_disadvantages: target is strongest against this approach
location, timing, or circumstances strongly favor the opposition

outcomes.critical: The first obstacle is already overcome; begin controlled at the next obstacle.
outcomes.6: Begin at the first obstacle in controlled position.
outcomes.4_5: Begin at the first obstacle in risky position.
outcomes.1_3: Begin at the first obstacle in desperate position.

engagement_roll.interpretation: A poor engagement result does not mean the crew planned incompetently. It means the capable opposition or circumstances have placed them in immediate danger.
engagement_roll.duration: The engagement result sets only the initial position. Set position normally after the first obstacle.

flashbacks.purpose: Reveal preparation only when it becomes relevant.
limits: A flashback cannot undo an established fact in the current fiction.
A flashback can establish a plausible past action, arrangement, or preparation.

stress_cost.1: Complex preparation or an unlikely opportunity.
stress_cost.2_or_more: Elaborate preparation requiring special opportunities, resources, or contingencies.

resolution: If success is uncertain and dangerous, make an action roll.
If only quality or extent is uncertain, make a fortune roll.
If the preparation is straightforward after paying stress, no roll is needed.

teamwork.assist: Take 1 stress, describe help, and give one teammate +1d. Only one direct assistant per roll.
teamwork.lead_group_action: All participating PCs roll the same action. Use the best result for everyone. The leader takes 1 stress for each participant whose best result is 1-3.
teamwork.protect: Take a consequence meant for a teammate and then resist it if desired.
teamwork.setup: Make an action that creates improved position or +1 effect for one or more follow-up actions.

score_loop: Describe the immediate obstacle and threat.
Ask what the PCs do and what result they want.
Resolve action rolls, resistance, teamwork, items, and flashbacks.
Advance or create clocks as consequences and effects require.
Show faction and NPC competence through fictional action, not hidden difficulty modifiers.
End when the operation's objective is resolved or the crew withdraws.

core_order: Heat: add exposure and update wanted level.
Entanglement: roll for underworld or legal fallout.
Downtime activities: each PC spends available activities.
Faction activity: advance relevant NPC clocks and communicate visible changes.
End-of-session advancement: review PC and crew XP triggers.

rep.tier_adjustment: Add or subtract 1 per Tier difference, minimum 0.

payoff.tithe: A stronger local boss may expect payment equal to crew Tier +1. Refusal may advance a patience clock and damage status.
payoff.principle: Do not negate earned payoff with an arbitrary betrayal or payment trap.

heat.wanted_threshold: At 9 heat, gain 1 wanted level, clear the heat track, and carry excess heat forward.
heat.wanted_effect: Higher wanted level makes law-enforcement responses and entanglements more severe.

entanglements.roll: Roll a number of dice equal to the crew's wanted level, including the zero-dice rule, then consult the current heat band.
entanglements.principle: The entanglement has already happened when introduced; the PCs decide how to answer it rather than preventing it retroactively.
handling_modes: Resolve quickly using the listed choices and costs.
Play the entanglement as a full scene using normal action and consequence procedures.

activity_allowance.normal: 2 free activities per PC after a score.
activity_allowance.extra: Each additional activity costs 1 coin or 1 rep.
activity_allowance.help: A friend or contact can grant +1d to a downtime roll when fictionally available.
activity_allowance.boost_after_roll: Spend 1 coin per result-level increase: 1-3 to 4/5, 4/5 to 6, or 6 to critical.

Acquire_Asset.purpose: Gain temporary use of an item, cohort, vehicle, or service.
Acquire_Asset.beyond_critical: Spend 2 coin per additional Tier of quality.
Acquire_Asset.restricted_item_heat: Acquiring restricted alchemicals, poisons, bombs, or dangerous gadgets adds 2 heat.
Acquire_Asset.duration: Usually one score or another single significant use.

Long_Term_Project.purpose: Advance a persistent personal, crew, investigative, social, technical, or supernatural goal.
Long_Term_Project.roll: Describe the work and roll an appropriate action.
Long_Term_Project.clock_size: The GM chooses one or more clocks according to complexity and required access.

Recover.roll: A healer rolls an appropriate action or NPC quality.
Recover.completion: When full, reduce every instance of harm by one level, clear the clock, and roll over extra ticks.
Recover.self_treatment: Take 2 stress and roll your own appropriate action.
Recover.new_harm: New harm clears progress on the healing clock.

Reduce_Heat.purpose: Explain how evidence, witnesses, or attention are suppressed.
Reduce_Heat.roll: Roll the action matching the method.

Train.purpose: Mark XP on an attribute or playbook track.
Train.limit: Each XP track may be trained only once per downtime.

Indulge_Vice.roll: Roll the lowest attribute rating and clear stress equal to the highest die.
Indulge_Vice.risk: Clearing more stress than marked causes overindulgence.

downtime.faction_downtime: Advance only the faction clocks that currently matter. Use Tier as a fortune roll if the amount of progress is uncertain, and tell players about visible changes through contacts, rumors, or direct events.

coin.meaning: An abstract unit of meaningful liquid wealth; ordinary pocket expenses are not tracked.
coin.carry_limit: A PC can normally keep 4 coin readily available; each coin physically carried as bulk currency consumes 1 load.
coin.crew_storage: A lair normally stores 4 coin, expandable by vault upgrades.

stash.purpose: Represents long-term wealth, lifestyle, and retirement prospects.
stash.deposit: Move coin into stash one-for-one when allowed by the sheet.
stash.lifestyle: Each complete row of 10 stash gives one lifestyle quality, from 0 to 4.

retirement_bands.40: Fine home, luxuries, and a stable business or equivalent.

incarceration.how_wanted_is_reduced: Someone is convicted and serves time for crimes associated with the crew. Reduce wanted level by 1 and clear heat.
incarceration.roll: Roll crew Tier after serving time.

outcomes.critical: Gain 3 rep, one prison claim, and +1 status with a faction assisted inside.
outcomes.6: Gain one prison claim and +1 status with a faction assisted inside.
outcomes.4_5: Serve the time without an additional mechanical result.

character_xp_during_play: Mark 1 XP in the relevant attribute whenever you make a desperate action roll, including participation in a desperate group action.
character_end_of_session_triggers: Addressed a challenge using the playbook's highlighted approach.
Expressed beliefs, drives, heritage, or background.
Struggled because of vice or trauma.
advancement.trigger_award: For each trigger, mark 1 XP if it occurred or 2 XP if it occurred repeatedly or strongly.
advancement.allocation: End-of-session XP may be placed on any character XP track unless a rule states otherwise.

character_advance.attribute_track: Add one dot to an action under that attribute.

crew_end_of_session_triggers: Completed the crew type's preferred operation or growth activity.
Contended with challenges above the crew's station.
Bolstered or developed the crew's reputation.
Expressed crew goals, drives, internal conflict, or essential nature.
advancement.crew_advance: When the crew XP track fills, choose one crew special ability or mark two crew upgrade boxes.
advancement.training: A downtime training activity marks 1 XP, or 2 with the matching crew training upgrade; each track may be trained once per downtime.

goals: Bring the city and its factions to life.
principles: Be a fan of the player characters without protecting them from consequences.
Let mechanics follow from established fiction.
Speak to both characters and players as appropriate.
Present haunted, industrial, crowded, dangerous surroundings.
Consider the actual risk before asking for a roll.
core_moves: Ask how the character does it and therefore which action is being used.
Cut to the moment of crisis.
State likely consequences and ask what the player does.
Create or tick a progress clock.
Ask players for details and build on their answers.
Let actions ripple through the faction network.
End with a clear prompt: what do you do?

prepare: A few factions with concrete goals and methods.
One or two visible opportunities per crew type.
NPCs with desires, leverage, and a preferred approach.
Locations with dangers, obstacles, and sensory details.
Potential clocks for complex threats or faction projects.
do_not_prepare: Secret difficulty numbers disconnected from the fiction.
An answer to every possible player question.

dangerous_npcs.ordinary: Resolve their threat through the PC's action roll.
dangerous_npcs.skilled: Use worse position, reduced effect, superior quality, potency, or scale.
dangerous_npcs.master_or_supernatural: The GM may require a resistance roll before the PC can act, representing the foe seizing initiative or imposing an immediate effect.
dangerous_npcs.rule: Explain what makes the opponent dangerous in the fiction rather than merely declaring a hidden penalty.

consequence_selection: Choose the consequence that directly follows from the threat described before the roll.
Use harm sparingly enough that other consequences remain meaningful.
Prefer complications, clocks, lost opportunities, and worse position when they create more interesting play.
Do not negate a successful action with its consequence.
State multiple consequences separately so the player can choose which to resist.
faction_management: Give each active faction a goal and method.
Advance only clocks that matter to current play.
Change faction status when operations materially help or hurt them.
Turn faction progress into rumors, offers, pressure, and scores.
Remember that every useful asset is likely claimed by someone.
spotlight_and_pacing: Cut between PCs when an action leaves someone in suspense.
Use group actions when everyone tackles the same obstacle.
Use setup and parallel scenes when characters contribute in different ways.
Skip uneventful travel and preparation; resume at a meaningful choice or threat.
Let a score end when its dramatic question is answered rather than forcing a target session length.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Planning the score in exhaustive detail.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.why_it_hurts: It slows play and asks players to predict problems that may never occur.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Choose the plan and required detail, then use engagement and flashbacks.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: The GM chooses the player's action rating.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.why_it_hurts: It removes the player's authority over method.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Ask what the PC does. The player chooses the action; the GM sets position and effect.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.why_it_hurts: Action rolls are for dangerous or troublesome opposition, not routine competence.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Say yes when there is no meaningful threat; use fortune only when uncertainty still matters.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.why_it_hurts: It confuses chance of success with severity of danger.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Position sets consequences; effect sets impact; the dice pool sets probabilities.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Using Tier as an automatic penalty to every roll.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.why_it_hurts: Tier matters only when quality or scale actually affects the described action.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Explain the relevant factor and adjust effect or position only when it matters.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: A 4/5 succeeds, then the consequence takes the success away.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Give the stated effect and add trouble that changes what happens next.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Forgetting resistance or presenting it as an uncertain defense.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.why_it_hurts: Resistance is a central player-control mechanism.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: After announcing consequences, explicitly ask whether the player resists; resistance always reduces or avoids.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Using only harm as a consequence.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.why_it_hurts: Harm accumulates slowly and can make downtime repetitive.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Rotate among clocks, heat, faction status, lost position, lost opportunity, gear trouble, and harm.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Calling for a separate NPC attack roll.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.why_it_hurts: The PC action roll already resolves both sides.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Express NPC action as the threat and apply it through position and consequences.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Keeping clocks abstract or secret without need.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Name what the clock means, show its progress, and state the consequence of completion.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.why_it_hurts: Downtime is where vice, relationships, factions, projects, and fallout become personal.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Frame brief scenes around meaningful choices, then move quickly through routine results.

common_mistakes_and_fixes.mistake: Mixing core and Deep Cuts procedures without labeling them.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.why_it_hurts: The modules change major subsystems and can create contradictions.
common_mistakes_and_fixes.fix: Record which version is active for Action, Harm and Trauma, Advancement, Downtime, and Load.

worked_examples.name: risky_infiltration
worked_examples.setup: A Lurk crosses a guarded courtyard to reach a second-story window. The goal is to reach the window unseen. The method is silent athletic movement, so the player chooses Prowl.
worked_examples.position_and_effect: The patrol makes the action risky. The courtyard is unusually wide, so the GM sets limited effect.
worked_examples.player_choice: The player trades position for effect, accepting desperate position for standard effect.
worked_examples.resolution: The Lurk reaches the window, but the GM advances an Alert clock by three segments as a serious complication. Because the action was desperate, the player marks 1 Prowess XP.
worked_examples.resistance: The player resists the clock consequence with Insight. The GM reduces the clock advance from three segments to one; the resistance roll determines stress.

worked_examples.name: social_mixed_success
worked_examples.setup: A Slide wants a clerk to grant access to restricted records. The player lies about being an inspector and chooses Sway.
worked_examples.position_and_effect: The forged identity is plausible, so the position is risky and effect is standard.
worked_examples.resolution: The clerk grants access. The GM does not revoke that success; instead, the clerk insists on accompanying the Slide, creating a new obstacle.

worked_examples.name: group_prowl
worked_examples.setup: Four PCs sneak through a warehouse together.
worked_examples.procedure: One PC leads a group Prowl action. All four roll Prowl; the best result applies to the whole group.
worked_examples.result: The best roll is 6, so everyone crosses successfully. Two participants rolled 1-3, so the leader takes 2 stress.

worked_examples.name: flashback_bribe
worked_examples.setup: During a score, the crew discovers a guard captain at an unexpected checkpoint.
worked_examples.flashback: A player declares that earlier they arranged for the captain's gambling debt to be purchased by a friendly broker.
worked_examples.cost: The GM calls this a complex but plausible opportunity and charges 1 stress.
worked_examples.roll: Because the captain's willingness is uncertain but the past arrangement itself is not dangerous, the GM uses a fortune roll.
worked_examples.result: On a 4/5, the captain allows passage but expects the debt to be erased immediately after the score.

worked_examples.name: downtime_recovery
worked_examples.setup: A PC has level-3 and level-1 harm and visits a quality-2 healer.
worked_examples.roll: The healer rolls 2d and gets 6, marking 3 segments on the 4-segment healing clock.
worked_examples.spend: The PC spends 1 coin to raise the result to critical, marking 5 segments.
worked_examples.resolution: The first four segments complete the clock, lowering every harm instance by one level. The fifth segment rolls over onto the cleared clock.

worked_examples.name: engagement
worked_examples.setup: The crew chooses a Deception plan to enter a secure gala using forged invitations.
worked_examples.pool: Start at 1d; add 1d because the detail exploits the target's reliance on guest lists; subtract 1d because a rival warned the staff. Roll 1d total.
worked_examples.opening: Begin in desperate position at the first real obstacle: the invitations pass the first desk, but a suspicious senior inspector is already questioning the crew in a private room.

steps: Spend 10-20 minutes on tone, boundaries, and the desired criminal activity.
Choose a crew type and rough reputation.
Create scoundrels, linking each friend, rival, vice, heritage, or background to at least one faction or local problem.
Finish crew creation, including hunting grounds, upgrades, contact, and status changes.
Present two or three immediate opportunities, each with a target, objective, likely opposition, and possible payoff.
Let the crew choose one opportunity and gather only enough information to select the plan detail.
Choose load, make engagement, and cut directly to the first obstacle.
Run 3-6 substantial obstacles, using a clock only when the obstacle is layered.
End the score when the objective is resolved or the crew withdraws.
Resolve payoff, heat, one entanglement, and two downtime activities per PC.
Review XP triggers and end on a new faction move or opportunity.

starter_opportunity_template.target: A modest faction holding something the crew wants.
starter_opportunity_template.objective: Steal, destroy, capture, protect, negotiate for, or transport one concrete asset.
starter_opportunity_template.complication: A second faction also wants the asset.
starter_opportunity_template.supernatural_element: Include one ghost, occult device, strange ward, or eerie location if the group wants the default setting's supernatural tone.
starter_opportunity_template.payoff: Use the standard 6-coin score benchmark unless the job is clearly smaller or larger.
clocks: A 4-segment obstacle clock for the main security layer.
A 4- or 6-segment danger clock for alert, pursuit, or supernatural escalation.

core_result.4_5: Success with consequence or partial result.

action_bonus_dice: +1d from one assistant who takes 1 stress.
+1d from either pushing for 2 stress or accepting a Devil's Bargain.
quick_reference.resistance_cost: 6 minus highest die; critical clears 1 stress.

deep_cuts_v1_2.relationship_to_core: An official setting and system expansion containing modular alternatives. It is not automatically the default edition of every Blades in the Dark campaign.
publicly_confirmed_content: diceless Downtime, including altered Vice, Healing, Crew Development, and Debt
v1_1_public_change_notes: Payoff was clarified to occur before Fallout in the Deep Cuts downtime sequence.
Some Heat numbers and wording were corrected.
The Work activity and Scoundrel downtime activities were clarified.
Cohort Tier advancement requirements were adjusted.
recommended_adoption: Learn the core game first unless the whole group explicitly wants the expansion.
Choose modules as a group rather than assuming all alternatives are active.
Record the active version beside each affected subsystem: Action, Harm and Trauma, Advancement, Downtime, and Load.
Use the Deep Cuts v1.2 book or its official sheets for exact procedures; this JSON intentionally does not reproduce the paid rules text.
deep_cuts_v1_2.compatibility_warning: Do not combine a core character sheet with selected Deep Cuts procedures unless all changed tracks, costs, and advancement fields are reconciled.

glossary.action: A named player-selected method such as Prowl, Sway, or Tinker.
glossary.action_rating: The number of dice normally rolled when using an action.
glossary.attribute: Insight, Prowess, or Resolve; mainly used for resistance and determined by breadth of action dots.
glossary.clock: A segmented tracker for progress or danger.
glossary.cohort: A gang or expert employed by the crew.
glossary.coin: An abstract unit of meaningful liquid wealth.
glossary.consequence: A harmful result following a threat or roll.
glossary.critical: A result with at least two sixes in a normal dice pool.
glossary.Devil's Bargain: A guaranteed complication accepted in exchange for +1d.
glossary.downtime: The phase after a score in which fallout and personal activities are resolved.
glossary.engagement: The fortune roll that establishes the opening position of a score.
glossary.faction_status: The crew's relationship with another faction, from -3 war to +3 allied.
glossary.Fine: An item quality advantage, normally one step above ordinary quality.
glossary.flashback: A past preparation introduced when it becomes relevant.
glossary.fortune_roll: A roll for uncertain outcomes when no action or resistance procedure applies.
glossary.harm: Persistent injury or debility with level-based penalties.
glossary.heat: Attention generated by the crew's crimes.
glossary.hold: How securely a faction occupies its current Tier.
glossary.load: The number of item slots a PC may reveal during a score and how conspicuous they appear.
glossary.playbook: A character or crew focus containing starting ratings, abilities, items, and XP triggers.
glossary.position: The danger level of an action: controlled, risky, or desperate.
glossary.potency: A special fictional advantage or especially effective force.
glossary.push: Spend 2 stress for a listed bonus.
glossary.resistance: A guaranteed reduction or avoidance of a consequence, with stress cost determined by a roll.
glossary.score: A criminal or daring operation with a concrete objective.
glossary.setup: A teamwork action that improves a follow-up action's position or effect.
glossary.stash: Long-term personal wealth and retirement security.
glossary.Tier: A faction or crew's broad scale, wealth, influence, and quality.
glossary.trauma: A permanent condition gained when the stress track fills.
glossary.turf: A claim that reduces the rep needed for crew development.
glossary.vice: A PC obsession used to clear stress during downtime.
glossary.wanted_level: The severity of sustained official attention; rises when heat reaches 9.

machine_use_notes.identifier_style: Human-readable section keys use snake_case where practical.
machine_use_notes.numbers: All numeric mechanics in this guide refer to the core rules unless the enclosing object is deep_cuts_v1_2.
rules_precedence: A specific playbook or crew ability overrides a general rule when it explicitly says so.
Established fiction determines whether a mechanic applies.
The official core book or active Deep Cuts module text controls any conflict with this educational summary.
